title: Lark Analytics / Redwood Discovery - Migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
summary: Discovery call to understand Lark's current OpenAI-based deployment, evaluate Redwood Dedicated/Private options, discuss compatibility (vLLM/TGI), eval parity concerns, and next steps for a benchmark pilot and security review.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jamie (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Tom (CTO - Lark), Maya (Head of MLOps), Evan (SRE)

[00:00] Jamie (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jamie Park, AE at Redwood. Priya and I will run through a few questions to understand your current OpenAI setup and what you're looking for on Dedicated/Private.
[00:12] Tom (Lark): Hi, Tom here. We appreciate the time. We're currently on OpenAI for most of our production calls, plus a small on-prem vLLM setup for cheaper embeddings, so kind of hybrid right now.
[00:25] Priya (Redwood): Great, can you tell us about traffic and latency targets? rough qps and 95th p50 etc?
[00:31] Maya (Lark): Sure, for the customer-facing chat we average about 150 rps during peak, p95 latency target is ~450ms for short prompts, but we also have longer retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) flows that can go beyond 5k tokens. Costs have been creeping up with OpenAI tokens — that's the main driver.
[00:47] Jamie (Redwood): Makes sense. When you say vLLM on-prem, is that TGI or vLLM proper? we've seen both, just want to map concretely to compat & runtime differences.
[00:55] Tom (Lark): It's vLLM with a couple of custom kernels. We tested TGI briefly but rolled back due to some stability things. Also we use a mix of models from OpenAI and some local open models for specific pipelines.
[01:08] Priya (Redwood): Got it. A few typical migration concerns: 1) API compatibility (will prompts/role tokens work the same), 2) eval parity — do your outputs match today, 3) latency/cost tradeoff on Dedicated, and 4) security/compliance like VPC, KMS and audit logs. Which is highest priority for you?
[01:25] Tom (Lark): Eval parity probably. If answers change, product behavior changes. Security is close second because we're in fintech and need strict audit trails. Cost is third but still important.
[01:36] Jamie (Redwood): Understood. Priya — want to talk through our compatibility story and the typical parity approach we take?
[01:40] Priya (Redwood): Sure — so Redwood exposes the same REST/SDK interface for hosted and dedicated. We have model variants and adapters for OpenAI-compatible request shapes, and we've done a bunch of migrations where we run A/B evals to validate output parity. That process usually includes a curated prompt set and statistical checks. There are occasional tokenization differences with some open models and those can affect scoring, but we document those and provide quant and kernel options to align behavior.
[02:05] Maya (Lark): When you say tokenization differences, do you mean things like different BPE splits causing varying completions? that's what bit us before when swapping models.
[02:11] Priya (Redwood): Exactly. For some models we see shifted completions because the context window tokens align differently; we often recommend small prompt rewrites or using a small post-processing alignment step. Also, we support running the same model family on our Dedicated pool so you can pin versions.
[02:26] Evan (Lark): On the infra side, how do you handle KV cache and warm starts? our RAG flows are sensitive to cold-start latency.
[02:32] Priya (Redwood): We have prefix/KV caching and continuous batching. On Dedicated you get predictable throughput and the runtime caches KV across requests per instance; we also support config for hot-shard pinning for critical routes. There can be slight differences in warm start times vs OpenAI, but because Dedicated is co-located on GPU pools you can often beat public APIs for p95 once the cache is primed.
[02:52] Tom (Lark): That sounds promising. For security: we require customer-managed KMS and VPC-only endpoints for any production PII traffic. Can Redwood do KMS integrations and a private control plane?
[03:04] Jamie (Redwood): Yes — Redwood Private provides a customer-managed control plane with VPC and on-prem options, and integrates with major KMS/HSM providers. We also provide audit logs and SSO/SAML for RBAC. For SOC 2 scope, we can share the cert and the detailed security pack.
[03:18] Maya (Lark): Good. Is there a data residency option? some of our EU customers require EU-only processing.
[03:23] Jamie (Redwood): We support region pinning and private deployments in EU regions; for dedicated we can ensure the instances and storage are in the region.
[03:30] Priya (Redwood): Back to eval parity: typical approach we recommend is a two-step pilot — first run a blind eval over a representative prompt set comparing OpenAI to Redwood Dedicated on the same model or a close variant, measure metrics (accuracy, hallucination rate, latency, cost). Then a short user-facing A/B test. For the blind eval we can run using the same tokenizer in our tooling to reduce preprocessing diffs.
[03:51] Tom (Lark): How long would a pilot take? and what's the effort from our side?
[03:55] Priya (Redwood): Usually 2-4 weeks for the blind eval and then another 2-6 weeks for a controlled A/B depending on traffic. From your side we'd need access to a set of prompts + expected outputs (or scoring metric), and environment access for the benchmark — we can do it against a staging dataset. We provide benchmark scripts and a result deck.
[04:12] Evan (Lark): Any gotchas around vLLM/TGI? We run a custom vLLM with kernel patches. Will code/weights port?
[04:19] Priya (Redwood): If you have custom kernel patches it's trickier; Redwood's runtime uses optimized kernels and sometimes quantized kernels that differ from vLLM. We can often match behavior by using the same model weights and careful quantization profiles, but custom vLLM kernel changes would need to be evaluated case-by-case. If necessary, we can run a compatibility test to check logits and token-level differences.
[04:39] Tom (Lark): Ok — and in terms of SLA and cost, how does Dedicated pricing look relative to usage-based OpenAI?
[04:45] Jamie (Redwood): Dedicated is reserved capacity pricing — usually a monthly commit for GPU pools. For high and predictable throughput it typically lowers unit cost by 30-60% depending on batching, KV cache benefits, and quantization. We can share a cost model spreadsheet — we did for other customers.
[05:01] Maya (Lark): Do you support autoscaling/burst capacity? We have traffic spikes.
[05:05] Jamie (Redwood): Yes, Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity options. For strict SLOs we can provision buffer capacity or multi-tier fallback to hosted model variants.
[05:16] Tom (Lark): Any migration timeline for a full cutover? We aren't expecting to flip a switch overnight, but want a rough migration plan.
[05:22] Priya (Redwood): Typical migration plan: 1) discovery & security review (1-2 weeks), 2) blind eval & benchmark (2-4 weeks), 3) pilot A/B (2-6 weeks), 4) staged rollouts with canaries and fallback (2-8 weeks), total commonly ~2-4 months depending on scope.
[05:38] Evan (Lark): For monitoring and observability — can we get token-level cost and per-route dashboards? We need traceability for costs by feature.
[05:45] Jamie (Redwood): Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-route/model dashboards, tracing hooks, and error analysis. We can give access to a trial console for the pilot.
[05:55] Tom (Lark): Great. Next steps — we'd want your SOC2, a proposed pricing sheet for Dedicated + Private options, and to kick off the blind eval. Also we need to check legal for data processing agreement.
[06:08] Jamie (Redwood): Makes sense. Priya, will follow up on technical checklist and benchmark scripts. We'll also send a pricing sketch and security pack.
[06:16] Priya (Redwood): I'll also add notes about tokenization diffs and recommended prompt rewrites.
[06:20] Maya (Lark): One more Q — do you have examples where customers moved from OpenAI to Redwood and retained eval parity? any win stories?
[06:27] Jamie (Redwood): Yes, we worked with a payments company that moved their fraud detection assistant; they ran a two-week blind eval, minor prompt tweaks and quantization profile adjustments gave them statistically similar outputs and reduced token costs by ~45%. We can share an anonymized case study.
[06:42] Tom (Lark): Awesome. Thanks everyone.
[06:45] Jamie (Redwood): Wrap-up: We'll send security docs, pricing, and benchmark scripts. Let's tentatively target kickoff for the blind eval next week if legal signs off.
[06:55] End of recording.

Transcription notes: occasional mis-hearings around kernel names (vLLM vs V L M spelled out), and 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache', minor punctuation dropouts.
